---
title: "Leading Without Being the Best Engineer in the Room"
date: 2026-09-21
categories: [Leadership, Career]
description: "Technical credibility for a product leader doesn't mean out-coding the team. It means asking better questions and making their work visible."
---

Early on, I thought technical credibility as a leader meant being the best engineer in the room — out-designing the architects, catching the edge cases, winning the design review. It took me too long to see what that actually buys you: a room full of engineers who've learned to wait for your answer instead of finding theirs.

The job isn't to be the best engineer in the room. Often you shouldn't even try — the team you've hired is better at it than you are. The job is to make the room *smarter* than it would be without you.

## What "technical" actually means for a leader

For a product or engineering leader, technical credibility is mostly about judgment, not syntax:

- **Asking the question nobody asked yet.** "What happens to this batch job when the experiment doubles write volume?" You don't need to fix it — you need to notice it before the incident does.
- **Understanding tradeoffs well enough to make them honestly.** Latency vs. cost, consistency vs. availability, ship-now vs. do-it-right. A leader who can't explain the tradeoff can't defend the decision later.
- **Smelling the risk.** Which part of this plan, if it goes wrong, takes the quarter with it? That's where the scrutiny belongs.

None of that requires being the strongest programmer present. All of it requires knowing enough to be dangerous — which comes from staying close to the work, not from proving you can do the work.

## Moves that earn trust

I've watched leaders build real technical credibility with a handful of repeatable behaviors:

- **Write things down.** The decision doc that captures *why* — including the options you rejected — is the single highest-leverage artifact a technical leader produces.
- **Read the design docs.** Not skim — read. Then ask the two questions that make it sharper.
- **Take the small Ls publicly.** When you got the call wrong, say so, quickly. Nothing buys credibility faster.
- **Give the work back.** "You know this system better than I do — what would you do?" is not a rhetorical device. Use it like one.

## The uncomfortable part

Here's the trap: proving you're the smartest person in the room is *gratifying*, and it's available every single meeting. Resisting it is a daily practice, not a one-time decision.

But the rooms where the leader makes everyone else better ship better products than the rooms where the leader wins the argument. That's the whole game — and it took me years to stop playing the wrong one.
